The Story of Satyaki and Jyeshtha

I bow to Lord Jina, whose eyes are omniscience, and I write the story of Satyaki and Jyeshtha according to the scriptures.

In the land of Gandhar stood the beautiful city of Maheshvarpur. Its king was Satyandhar, whose beloved wife was Satyvati. They had a son named Satyaki, who became skilled in the arts of statecraft — for without such knowledge, a prince cannot shine.

At this time, Chetak was king of the city of Vishala in Sindh. He was a protector of Jain dharma and a true devotee of Lord Jinendra. His queen was Subhadra, a devoted and virtuous wife. They had seven daughters: Pavitra, Mrigavati, Suprabha, Prabhavati, Chelini, Jyeshtha, and Chandana.

Emperor Shrenik had asked Chetak for Chelini's hand, but Chetak, seeing that Shrenik was too old, refused. This grieved Shrenik deeply. His son Abhay Kumar, learning of his father's sorrow, had an exquisite portrait of Shrenik painted and carried it to Vishala. He showed it to Chelini and won her heart. But Chelini's father would not consent to her marriage with Shrenik. So Abhay Kumar planned to take her away secretly. When Chelini agreed to go with him, her sister Jyeshtha asked to be taken along. Chelini agreed, though she did not truly wish it. When the two sisters had gone some distance, the cunning Chelini said to Jyeshtha, "Sister, I have left all my ornaments in the palace. Would you go and fetch them? I shall wait here." Poor innocent Jyeshtha fell for the trick and turned back. As soon as she had gone a short distance, Chelini took the other path and sped far ahead. By the time Jyeshtha reached the meeting place, Chelini was long gone.

Jyeshtha was deeply wounded by her sister's deceit. In her grief, she went to the nun Yashvati and took the vow of renunciation. Meanwhile, Jyeshtha had been betrothed to Satyaki, the son of King Satyandhar. When Satyaki heard that she had become a nun, he too was moved to renunciation and became a monk under the sage Samadhi Gupt.

One day, the nun Yashvati, Jyeshtha, and other nuns were travelling when they encountered dangers on the road. Satyaki, now a monk, happened to be in the same region. Through the power of their spiritual practice and mutual example of renunciation, both Jyeshtha and Satyaki advanced on the path of liberation. They practised austerities with great dedication, destroyed their karmas, and ultimately attained the supreme state of moksha.

This story teaches that even betrayal and worldly disappointment can become the gateway to spiritual awakening. Jyeshtha's suffering at her sister's hands freed her from worldly bonds, and Satyaki, inspired by her renunciation, followed the same path. What the world calls misfortune, the wise recognise as opportunity.
